key_insight: Disordered metal-oxide photonic glasses can produce architectural colors in photovoltaics without pigments or strong iridescence, but the achievable hue and stability depend strongly on oxide choice, encapsulant, and viewing geometry.
engineering_relevance: This work provides a design map for color-tuned building-integrated photovoltaics that balances aesthetic targets with optical performance, highlighting which materials can deliver specific facade colors with minimal photocurrent penalty.
method: Combined Mie scattering with the Percus–Yevick structure factor to model disordered nanosphere optics.
Used exact phase functions plus two-flux transfer, including absorption and refraction in the front glass.
Swept oxide type, particle size, packing fraction, layer number, encapsulant, and cell technology to target four named colors.
evidence_signal: The authors report that all four target colors were achieved in a laminated three-layer coating with DeltaE00 around 0.8 to 2.5, while angle tests showed daily color drift of about 5 to 18 DeltaE00.
watch_item: Angle-independent color is not guaranteed: facade geometry and sun/viewing angle can shift the perceived color substantially, so optical design must be co-optimized for installation conditions.
paper_title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
